contents.html: This report summarizes the feedback received on the work of the NIST Cybersecurity for IoT program on device cybersecurity at a virtual workshop in July 2020. NISTIR 8259, Foundational Cybersecurity Activities for IoT Device Manufacturers and NISTIR 8259A, IoT Device Cybersecurity Capability Core Baseline provide general guidance on how manufacturers can understand and approach their role in supporting customers’ cybersecurity needs and goals. As discussed in those documents, specific sectors and use cases may require more specific guidance than what is included in NISTIR 8259A’s core baseline for IoT devices. NIST conducted the virtual workshop “Building the Federal Profile for IoT Device Cybersecurity” to discuss and gather community input on the creation of a federal profile of the core baseline for use by federal agencies. This publication provides a summary of the workshop. The baseline will be published in NISTIR 8259D, Profile of the IoT Core Baseline for the Federal Government.
contents.html_ja: 本報告書は、2020年7月に開催されたバーチャルワークショップで、NIST の Cybersecurity for IoT プログラムによるデバイスのサイバーセキュリティに関する取り組みに対して寄せられたフィードバックをまとめたものです。NISTIR 8259, Foundational Cybersecurity Activities for IoT Device Manufacturers と NISTIR 8259A, IoT Device Cybersecurity Capability Core Baseline は、製造者が顧客のサイバーセキュリティ上のニーズと目標を支援する自らの役割をどのように理解し、取り組めばよいかについて、一般的なガイダンスを提供しています。これらの文書で論じられているように、特定の分野やユースケースでは、NISTIR 8259A の IoT デバイス向けコアベースラインに含まれるものよりも具体的なガイダンスが必要になる場合があります。NIST は、連邦機関が使用するためのコアベースラインの連邦プロファイルの作成について議論し、コミュニティから意見を収集するため、バーチャルワークショップ「Building the Federal Profile for IoT Device Cybersecurity」を実施しました。本刊行物は、そのワークショップの概要を示します。このベースラインは、NISTIR 8259D, Profile of the IoT Core Baseline for the Federal Government として公開される予定です。

contents.html: On July 22-23, 2020, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) conducted a virtual workshop entitled Building the Federal Profile For IoT Device Cybersecurity: Next Steps for Securing Federal Systems. The event included stakeholders from across government, industry, international bodies, and academia. The goal was to identify gaps in the Internet of Things (IoT) cybersecurity ecosystem that need to be addressed in a federal profile for IoT device cybersecurity. Over 500 people participated from the U.S. and 25 other countries, representing a broad mix of government, industry, and academia.

contents.html: The mission of the NIST Cybersecurity for the Internet of Things (IoT) program [PRGM] is to cultivate trust in the IoT and foster an environment that enables innovation on a global scale through standards, guidance, and related tools. The Cybersecurity for IoT program supports the development and application of standards, guidelines, and related tools to improve the cybersecurity of connected devices and the environments in which they are deployed. By collaborating with stakeholders across government, industry, international bodies, and academia, the program aims to cultivate trust and foster an environment that enables innovation on a global scale.

contents.html: NIST leveraged the Core Baseline established in NIST Internal Report (NISTIR) 8259A, IoT Device Cybersecurity Capability Core Baseline [NISTIR8259A], and analyzed the security controls found in NIST Special Publication (SP) 800-53, Security and Privacy Controls for Federal Information Systems and Organizations [SP800-53], to develop a catalog of key IoT device cybersecurity capabilities and non-technical supporting capabilities and associated IoT device customer controls. As was discussed in NISTIR 8228, Considerations for Managing Internet of Things (IoT) Cybersecurity and Privacy Risks [NISTIR8228], IoT devices routinely lack critical cybersecurity capabilities that are commonly found in IT devices. Additionally, IoT manufacturers often do not provide sufficient information for IoT device customers to integrate their devices in secure ways in order to mitigate the risks created within the associated systems and to comply with compliance requirements. The catalog under development is a critical building block for establishing a federal profile of the Core Baseline (“federal profile”) to help federal agencies and manufacturers bridge these gaps. Identifying critically needed capabilities will help federal agencies acquire IoT devices that they can securely incorporate into their systems and meet security requirements for federal information and systems. The future federal profile also aims to help manufacturers looking at federal customers and use cases to go beyond identifying the types of cybersecurity device capabilities listed in NISTIR 8259A to considering specific capabilities requirements of federal agencies. Manufacturers can engineer the technical capabilities and provide non-technical supporting capabilities to IoT device customers to help ensure that customers’ systems meet an established level of management, operational, and technical security control requirements.
contents.html_ja: NIST は、NIST Internal Report（NISTIR）8259A, IoT Device Cybersecurity Capability Core Baseline [NISTIR8259A] で確立されたコアベースラインを活用し、NIST Special Publication（SP）800-53, Security and Privacy Controls for Federal Information Systems and Organizations [SP800-53] にあるセキュリティ管理策を分析して、IoT デバイスの主要なサイバーセキュリティ能力、非技術的な支援能力、および関連する IoT デバイス顧客向け管理策のカタログを作成しました。NISTIR 8228, Considerations for Managing Internet of Things (IoT) Cybersecurity and Privacy Risks [NISTIR8228] で論じられたように、IoT デバイスには、IT デバイスで一般的に見られる重要なサイバーセキュリティ能力が欠けていることがよくあります。さらに、IoT 製造者は、IoT デバイスの顧客が関連システム内に生じるリスクを軽減し、コンプライアンス要件を満たすために、デバイスを安全に統合するための十分な情報を提供しないことがよくあります。策定中のこのカタログは、連邦機関と製造者がこれらのギャップを埋める助けとなる、コアベースラインの連邦プロファイル（「連邦プロファイル」）を確立するための重要な構成要素です。特に必要とされる能力を特定することで、連邦機関は、自らのシステムに安全に組み込むことができ、連邦の情報およびシステムに関するセキュリティ要件を満たす IoT デバイスを取得しやすくなります。将来の連邦プロファイルは、連邦の顧客やユースケースに関心を持つ製造者が、NISTIR 8259A に挙げられたデバイスのサイバーセキュリティ能力の種類を特定するだけでなく、連邦機関に固有の能力要件を検討する助けとなることも目指しています。製造者は、技術的能力を設計し、非技術的な支援能力を IoT デバイスの顧客に提供することで、顧客のシステムが、確立された水準の管理面、運用面、技術面のセキュリティ管理策要件を満たすことを確実にする助けとなれます。

contents.html: These takeaways are ideas that NIST heard from participants and that received significant support from attendees and/or panelists. This workshop was not a forum for developing consensus, so these takeaways represent themes repeatedly heard not a formal position of attendees or participants. While this document seeks to be thorough in reflecting the workshop discussions, a summary document cannot capture all the thoughts, opinions, and suggestions provided during the sessions. The topics, takeaways, and observations in this report do not represent specific NIST recommendations or guidance, but are intended to capture and summarize discussions from the workshop and viewpoints expressed by panelists and participants. These takeaways provide important feedback to the program and a basis for future conversations with the community.

The General Services Administration (GSA) has identified over 75 makes and 210 distinct models of IoT devices deployed in facilities they manage, spanning a broad range of IoT related services. contents.html: Manufacturers have entered the IoT market with enthusiasm leading to a great deal of innovation and a diversity of product offerings. However, this market is still quite immature and dynamic where price and features have dominated manufacturer priorities and cybersecurity has not been given adequate attention. Many small- and medium-size manufacturers moving into the IoT market do not have the cybersecurity background of more established information technology (IT) product manufacturers. Many of the lessons learned in the world of security for IT have not yet been applied to IoT devices, or haven’t been adapted to those devices’ unique characteristics, such as limited power and computing capabilities. The market is also quite diverse, with some vertical sectors (e.g., medical devices) having more clearly defined requirements than others (e.g., consumer-oriented IoT).
contents.html_ja: 製造者は熱意をもって IoT 市場に参入しており、大きなイノベーションと多様な製品の提供につながっています。しかし、この市場はまだ非常に未成熟で流動的であり、価格と機能が製造者の優先事項を占め、サイバーセキュリティには十分な注意が払われていません。IoT 市場に参入する多くの中小規模の製造者は、より確立した情報技術（IT）製品の製造者ほどのサイバーセキュリティの素養を持っていません。IT のセキュリティの世界で得られた教訓の多くは、まだ IoT デバイスに適用されていないか、電力や計算能力が限られているといったこれらのデバイス固有の特性に合わせて調整されていません。この市場は非常に多様でもあり、一部の垂直分野（たとえば医療機器）は、他の分野（たとえば消費者向け IoT）よりも要件が明確に定義されています。

contents.html: While IoT devices are becoming nearly ubiquitous in many environments, defining and categorizing such devices remains an on-going challenge.<sup>3</sup> IoT covers a broad spectrum, from building monitoring systems to connected automobiles to smart appliances and even toys. This lack of consensus was discussed at the October 2017 NIST IoT Cybersecurity Colloquium. Since that event, the NIST IoT Cybersecurity program published a description of IoT device capabilities in NISTIR 8228, and created a working definition of IoT devices as the scope for NISTIR 8259. Panelists in the July 2020 workshop, including representatives from two vendor participants, described the NISTIR 8259 characterization of IoT devices as having “at least one transducer (sensor or actuator) for interacting directly with the physical world and at least one network interface … for interfacing with the digital world” as “more or less becom[ing] a de facto definition … [that] will probably be used by regulatory bodies in the U.S. and the federal government and abroad moving forward.”<sup>4</sup>
contents.html_ja: IoT デバイスは多くの環境でほぼ遍在するようになっていますが、そのようなデバイスの定義と分類は依然として継続的な課題です。<sup>3</sup> IoT は、建物の監視システムからコネクテッドカー、スマート家電、さらには玩具に至るまで、幅広い範囲に及びます。この合意の欠如は、2017年10月の NIST IoT Cybersecurity Colloquium で議論されました。そのイベント以降、NIST IoT Cybersecurity プログラムは、NISTIR 8228 で IoT デバイスの能力の記述を公表し、NISTIR 8259 の対象範囲として IoT デバイスの作業上の定義を作成しました。2020年7月のワークショップのパネリスト（ベンダー 2 社の代表を含む）は、「物理世界と直接やり取りするトランスデューサー（センサーまたはアクチュエーター）を少なくとも 1 つ、デジタル世界とのインタフェースとなるネットワークインタフェースを少なくとも 1 つ」持つものとする NISTIR 8259 の IoT デバイスの特徴づけについて、「多かれ少なかれ事実上の定義になりつつあり、今後、米国の規制当局や連邦政府、そして海外でも使われる可能性が高い」と述べました。<sup>4</sup>

contents.html: Takeaway 3: IoT customers, especially in the consumer space, tend not to prioritize IoT device security and are often unaware that it should be a consideration in their selection and use of IoT devices.

contents.html: Overwhelmingly, workshop participants agreed that customers lack an awareness that cybersecurity capabilities can vary among devices when they make purchasing decisions about IoT. This appears to be true regardless of whether the customers are individual consumers or those responsible for procurement in organizational environments. In the consumer space the buyer’s assumption generally is that if a product is on the market, its safety and security can be assumed. A UK study found that consumers focus on IoT device features and costs as the most important discriminators, with cybersecurity either not on the list of customer priorities or at best lagging far behind as a decision criterion. Mike Bergman of the Consumer Technology Association (CTA) stated that “we have been doing this research for years and years and the answers never changed. Cybersecurity is not on this list. So while it might be a good idea to try to get it on the list … it is going to be a very long and expensive education process.”
contents.html_ja: ワークショップの参加者は圧倒的に、顧客が IoT の購入を決定する際に、サイバーセキュリティ能力がデバイスによって異なりうることを認識していないという点で一致しました。これは、顧客が個人の消費者であるか、組織環境で調達を担当する者であるかを問わず当てはまるようです。消費者分野では、購入者は一般に、製品が市場に出ているならその安全性とセキュリティは前提としてよいと考えています。英国の調査では、消費者は IoT デバイスの機能とコストを最も重要な判断材料として重視しており、サイバーセキュリティは顧客の優先事項の一覧に入っていないか、入っていても判断基準としては大きく後れをとっていることがわかりました。Consumer Technology Association（CTA）の Mike Bergman 氏は、「私たちは何年も何年もこの調査を行ってきましたが、答えは変わりません。サイバーセキュリティはこの一覧に入っていません。ですから、それを一覧に入れようとするのはよい考えかもしれませんが、…非常に長く費用のかかる教育のプロセスになるでしょう」と述べました。

contents.html: Where meaningful cybersecurity information about a product is available, a further challenge is educating customers about how to understand the information available and interpret its implications when using the product in their environments. In organizational procurement environments, the staff responsible for procurement contracts typically lack subject matter expertise regarding cybersecurity and need education and training in leveraging contractual language to mandate security for procurements. Peter Stephens said “whenever I speak to procurement organizations, whether they are retailers or housing, manufacturing, builders or other organizations who use smart devices in some format, the person responsible for procuring the devices quite often is not an expert at all.” The availability of sample procurement language can be of great benefit in improving the security of products procured by organizations.
contents.html_ja: 製品に関する有意義なサイバーセキュリティ情報が入手できる場合でも、入手可能な情報をどう理解し、自らの環境で製品を使用する際の意味合いをどう解釈するかを顧客に教育することが、さらなる課題となります。組織の調達環境では、調達契約を担当する職員は通常、サイバーセキュリティに関する専門知識を欠いており、調達にセキュリティを義務づけるために契約文言を活用する方法についての教育とトレーニングを必要としています。Peter Stephens 氏は、「小売業者であれ、住宅、製造、建設業者であれ、何らかの形でスマートデバイスを使用するその他の組織であれ、調達組織と話すときはいつも、デバイスの調達を担当する人が専門家でないことが非常に多い」と述べました。調達文言のサンプルが利用できれば、組織が調達する製品のセキュリティを向上させるうえで大きな利点となりえます。

contents.html: Most workshop participants agreed that manufacturers of IoT devices currently lack market incentives to prioritize cybersecurity as a concern when designing, marketing, and supporting their products. Some counterexamples were presented in which informed customers do recognize the advantages of enhanced security. This suggests that enhanced cybersecurity could demonstrably be a market advantage if it is emphasized. Workshop poll results showed strong support (71 %) for government mandates as a mechanism for enhancing IoT cybersecurity (poll #4), and general agreement (55 %) that developers of IoT devices currently lack appropriate incentives to secure their products (poll #2). Participants supported a mixture of regulatory guidance, customer education, supply chain pressures, and other considerations to create the economic incentives to shift the overall IoT device market toward enhanced cybersecurity.
contents.html_ja: ワークショップの参加者の大半は、IoT デバイスの製造者には現在、製品の設計、販売、サポートの際にサイバーセキュリティを懸念事項として優先する市場のインセンティブが欠けているという点で一致しました。情報を得た顧客が、強化されたセキュリティの利点を認識している反例もいくつか示されました。これは、サイバーセキュリティの強化が、強調すれば市場上の優位性になりうる可能性を示唆しています。ワークショップの投票結果では、IoT のサイバーセキュリティを強化する仕組みとして政府による義務づけに強い支持（71 %）があり（投票 #4）、IoT デバイスの開発者には現在、自社製品を保護する適切なインセンティブがないという点で概ね一致（55 %）しました（投票 #2）。参加者は、IoT デバイス市場全体をサイバーセキュリティの強化に向かわせる経済的インセンティブを生み出すため、規制上のガイダンス、顧客の教育、サプライチェーンからの圧力、その他の考慮事項を組み合わせることを支持しました。

contents.html: A lack of customer understanding today often translates into a lack of demand for needed device cybersecurity capabilities, leading to manufacturers prioritizing other aspects when defining their markets and developing products. The lack of incentives to address cybersecurity is a significant problem in the current IoT ecosystem. This lack is particularly problematic with new developers of IoT devices, who are focused on features and fail to recognize their responsibilities for cybersecurity, and with smaller developers who lack the resources, and often the awareness of the need for cybersecurity, to engineer cybersecurity capabilities within their IoT devices. The introduction of third-party certification or labeling authorities into the ecosystem could also provide incentives for IoT device developers and help level the playing field by encouraging all developers to address cybersecurity requirements.
contents.html_ja: 現在の顧客の理解不足は、必要なデバイスのサイバーセキュリティ能力への需要の不足につながることが多く、製造者は市場を定め製品を開発する際に他の側面を優先することになります。サイバーセキュリティに取り組むインセンティブの欠如は、現在の IoT エコシステムにおける重大な問題です。この欠如は、機能に集中してサイバーセキュリティに対する自らの責任を認識しない IoT デバイスの新規開発者や、IoT デバイスにサイバーセキュリティ能力を組み込む資源を持たず、サイバーセキュリティの必要性への認識も乏しいことの多い小規模な開発者にとって、特に問題となります。エコシステムに第三者認証や表示の機関を導入することも、IoT デバイスの開発者にインセンティブを与え、すべての開発者にサイバーセキュリティ要件への対応を促すことで、競争条件の平準化に役立つ可能性があります。

contents.html: The requirement for government purchasers to meet mandatory security requirements provides some degree of incentive but the government market, including both civil government and DoD, is neither large enough nor diverse enough to have sufficient leverage to truly drive the broader IoT market. Panel members also mentioned a variety of proposals for incentives to improve IoT device cybersecurity: legislative solutions, third-party certifications, and non-profit labeling authorities. All of these approaches were recognized as ways to encourage manufacturer attention to cybersecurity. A primary objective for all of these incentives is to encourage the development of a trusted, international marketplace for IoT devices where the customers can confidently procure IoT devices and manufacturers recognize that cybersecurity as a feature has meaningful market value.
contents.html_ja: 政府の購入者に必須のセキュリティ要件を満たすことが求められることは、ある程度のインセンティブになりますが、文民の政府機関と DoD の両方を含む政府市場は、より広い IoT 市場を真に動かす十分な影響力を持つほど大きくも多様でもありません。パネリストはまた、IoT デバイスのサイバーセキュリティを向上させるインセンティブについて、立法による解決策、第三者認証、非営利の表示機関といったさまざまな案に言及しました。これらのアプローチはいずれも、製造者のサイバーセキュリティへの注意を促す方法として認識されました。これらすべてのインセンティブの主要な目的は、顧客が安心して IoT デバイスを調達でき、製造者がサイバーセキュリティという機能に意味のある市場価値があることを認識する、信頼できる国際的な IoT デバイス市場の発展を促すことです。

contents.html: Workshop participants were broadly supportive of the development and application of formal guidance as a mechanism to improve the cybersecurity of IoT devices. This guidance is developing in the form of international standards, national and state government legislation and regulations, and other mechanisms. Several examples of such guidance were discussed. The NIST IoT cybersecurity program in the U.S. is developing guidance that can be applied by federal agencies, as well as other sectors that choose to adopt them. Individual U.S. states have begun developing IoT security regulations, mandating specific security features in state laws. The United Kingdom is legislating IoT cybersecurity requirements.
contents.html_ja: ワークショップの参加者は、IoT デバイスのサイバーセキュリティを向上させる仕組みとして、正式なガイダンスの策定と適用を広く支持しました。このガイダンスは、国際標準、国および州政府の法律と規制、その他の仕組みという形で整備が進んでいます。そのようなガイダンスの例がいくつか議論されました。米国の NIST IoT サイバーセキュリティプログラムは、連邦機関のほか、ガイダンスの採用を選択した他の分野でも適用できるガイダンスを策定しています。米国の個々の州は、州法で特定のセキュリティ機能を義務づける IoT セキュリティ規制の策定を始めています。英国は、IoT のサイバーセキュリティ要件を立法化しています。

contents.html: In addition to governmental cybersecurity standardization and regulation efforts within the U.S. at the national and state level, international standards bodies are working to establish IoT cybersecurity guidance, such as the development of International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission (ISO/IEC) 27402, Cybersecurity — IoT security and privacy — Device baseline requirements. The development of consensus international standards could provide a baseline of cybersecurity guidance for manufacturers and assist in the development of a trusted international marketplace.

contents.html_ja: 要点 6: 製造者は、複数の情報源からの断片化したガイダンスによって、製品の提供も断片化せざるをえなくなるのではないかと懸念しています。

contents.html: Manufacturing representatives expressed concern about the potential with the proliferation of guidance from multiple sources for creating conflicting requirements, creating the potential that manufacturers will be forced to respond to fragmented and incompatible or contradictory guidance from different jurisdictions. In that situation manufacturers are faced with the challenge of deciding which markets to address and which regulations apply within those markets. Manufacturers want regulatory consistency and are challenged if conflicting requirements from diverse sources necessitate costly measures (e.g., multiple manufacturing lines) in order to deliver products that address the relevant guidance. Trevor Rudolph said “from the manufacturer’s standpoint really what we want is regulatory certainty and guidance from the federal government.” The ability to focus resources on improving cybersecurity overall by creating fewer products suitable for a broader set of markets is diminished if fragmented regulatory guidance enforces a need to provide different versions of products that each satisfy a different guidance regime. Gordan Gillerman stated “In my experience, manufacturers are adept at building products that meet supersets of requirements and having them be globally able. What is challenging for manufacturers is when all of a sudden [they] need two production lines for the same product because somebody has exclusive requirements from what everyone else agreed on.” Specific security measures that do not adapt to the evolving technology of IoT devices create additional potential for market fragmentation.
contents.html_ja: 製造側の代表者は、複数の情報源からのガイダンスが急増することで、相反する要件が生じ、製造者が、異なる管轄区域からの断片化した、互換性のない、または矛盾するガイダンスへの対応を迫られる可能性があることへの懸念を表明しました。そのような状況では、製造者は、どの市場に対応するか、それぞれの市場でどの規制が適用されるかを決めるという課題に直面します。製造者は規制の一貫性を求めており、多様な情報源からの相反する要件のために、関連するガイダンスに対応した製品を提供するのに費用のかかる措置（たとえば複数の製造ライン）が必要になれば、困難に直面します。Trevor Rudolph 氏は、「製造者の立場から本当に望むのは、規制の確実性と連邦政府からのガイダンスです」と述べました。断片化した規制上のガイダンスにより、それぞれ異なるガイダンスの体系を満たす異なるバージョンの製品を提供する必要が生じると、より広い市場に適した少数の製品を作ることによって、サイバーセキュリティ全体の向上に資源を集中する能力が損なわれます。Gordan Gillerman 氏は、「私の経験では、製造者は要件の上位集合を満たし、世界中で使える製品を作ることに長けています。製造者にとって困難なのは、他のみんなが合意した内容と相容れない要件を誰かが持っているために、突然、同じ製品に 2 本の生産ラインが必要になる場合です」と述べました。IoT デバイスの進化する技術に適応しない特定のセキュリティ対策は、市場の断片化をさらに生じさせる可能性があります。

contents.html: Takeaway 7: Security for IoT is a shared responsibility between manufacturers and customers. The goal of a shared responsibility is: Manufacturers provide securable products and guidance on secure configuration and use. Customers then apply the manufacturer’s guidance to employ the technology securely.
contents.html_ja: 要点 7: IoT のセキュリティは、製造者と顧客の共同責任です。共同責任の目標は次のとおりです。製造者は、セキュリティ保護可能な製品と、セキュアな構成および使用に関するガイダンスを提供します。そして顧客は、製造者のガイダンスを適用して、その技術をセキュアに使用します。

contents.html: Security for IoT devices cannot be achieved through technology alone. Eighty-two percent of responses to one poll question agreed that the responsibility for securing IoT devices is shared between manufacturer and customer (poll #9). On the manufacturer side, devices should incorporate appropriate technical cybersecurity capabilities so that secure deployment and operation are feasible, and those technical capabilities should be complemented with non-technical supporting capabilities such as documentation explaining secure configurations, software updates to address discovered vulnerabilities, and publication of security best practices for their products. Customers, then, are responsible for implementing IoT devices in accordance with manufacturer guidance, ensuring devices have connectivity to receive updates, and monitoring devices to ensure continued security. Customers also follow their own established policies to appropriately mitigate the risks that IoT devices bring within their system(s). The support procedures will typically use the manufacturer’s guidance. Bo Berlas suggested that a solution similar to FedRAMP would be appropriate: “in cloud with FedRAMP there is this notion of customer responsibility such that what the vendor does together with what the customer does effectively results in a secure profile and I think that logic can generally align here too.”
contents.html_ja: IoT デバイスのセキュリティは、技術だけでは達成できません。あるアンケートの質問への回答の 82 パーセントが、IoT デバイスを保護する責任は製造者と顧客で共有されることに同意しました（アンケート #9）。製造者の側では、セキュアな展開と運用が実現可能となるよう、デバイスに適切な技術的サイバーセキュリティ能力を組み込むべきです。そして、その技術的な能力を、セキュアな構成を説明する文書、発見された脆弱性に対処するソフトウェア更新、自社製品のセキュリティのベストプラクティスの公開といった、非技術的な支援能力で補完すべきです。そのうえで顧客は、製造者のガイダンスに従って IoT デバイスを実装し、更新を受け取るための接続性をデバイスが備えていることを確保し、継続的なセキュリティを確保するためにデバイスを監視する責任を負います。顧客はまた、自ら確立したポリシーに従い、IoT デバイスが自らのシステム内にもたらすリスクを適切に軽減します。支援のための手順は通常、製造者のガイダンスを利用します。Bo Berlas 氏は、FedRAMP に似た解決策が適切であると示唆しました。「クラウドの FedRAMP には顧客の責任という考え方があり、ベンダーが行うことと顧客が行うことが相まって、結果的にセキュアなプロファイルになります。この論理は、ここでも概ね当てはまると思います。」

contents.html: Takeaway 8: Manufacturer support for IoT device security is essential for the shared responsibility model to succeed.
contents.html_ja: 要点 8: 共同責任モデルが成功するには、IoT デバイスのセキュリティに対する製造者の支援が不可欠です。

contents.html: Manufacturer support comprises a number of activities, especially documentation and software updates. An on-going challenge for customers and users in assessing and improving IoT device cybersecurity is inadequate documentation of device characteristics. Lack of documentation hinders both security assessments and the ability to select compensating security controls to address IoT device cybersecurity shortcomings. While some manufacturers do provide substantive documentation, many provide very little, leaving customer organizations starved for information on which to base risk assessments. Both the development of security solutions and the assessment of those solutions require information about, for example, the network communications patterns expected for IoT devices.
contents.html_ja: 製造者の支援は、特に文書化とソフトウェア更新を中心に、多くの活動からなります。顧客と利用者が IoT デバイスのサイバーセキュリティを評価し向上させる際の継続的な課題は、デバイスの特性に関する文書化が不十分なことです。文書の欠如は、セキュリティ評価と、IoT デバイスのサイバーセキュリティ上の欠点に対処する代替のセキュリティ管理策を選択する能力の両方を妨げます。製造者の中には実質的な文書を提供しているところもありますが、提供される文書がごくわずかな製造者も多く、顧客組織はリスクアセスメントの根拠とする情報に飢えた状態に置かれています。セキュリティ解決策の開発も、その解決策の評価も、たとえば IoT デバイスに想定されるネットワーク通信のパターンに関する情報を必要とします。

contents.html: Manufacturer communications regarding IoT device cybersecurity need to address a range of audiences with diverse levels of sophistication and understanding of the cybersecurity challenge. This includes communication both at the consumer level and with organizational procurement activities. Vendors need to convey information about product operation and about using device cybersecurity features, as well as more general communications regarding manufacturer procedures and commitments for vulnerability disclosure, software update frequency and mechanisms, and duration of support commitments for IoT products. Derail Heiland explained “we need to be able to get detailed information around those specific security topics on how do we reduce risk by properly implementing. How do we deploy into our organization? How do we get the detailed information to help us make those security risks evaluations for better deploying the technology? Often we are not seeing that information.”
contents.html_ja: IoT デバイスのサイバーセキュリティに関する製造者のコミュニケーションは、サイバーセキュリティ上の課題に対する洗練度や理解度が多様な、幅広い対象者に向けたものである必要があります。これには、消費者レベルでのコミュニケーションと、組織の調達活動に対するコミュニケーションの両方が含まれます。ベンダーは、製品の動作とデバイスのサイバーセキュリティ機能の使用に関する情報を伝える必要があるほか、脆弱性の開示、ソフトウェア更新の頻度と仕組み、IoT 製品のサポート提供期間のコミットメントに関する製造者の手順とコミットメントについて、より一般的なコミュニケーションも行う必要があります。Derail Heiland 氏は次のように説明しました。「私たちは、適切に実装することでリスクをどう減らすかについて、それらの特定のセキュリティトピックに関する詳細な情報を得られる必要があります。組織にどう展開すればよいのか。この技術をよりよく展開するためのセキュリティリスクの評価に役立つ詳細な情報を、どう入手すればよいのか。多くの場合、そうした情報が見当たりません。」

contents.html: An essential element of manufacturer communications is clear explanation of customer responsibilities for IoT device cybersecurity. Consumers, for example, primarily need basic installation and configuration guidance, whereas organizational customers need more extensive documentation to address device configurability, deployment of devices at scale, and information enabling the organization to ensure it is able to satisfy its legal obligations. All customers need clarity regarding available manufacturer communications channels, frequency of software updates, and end-of-life dates beyond which specific IoT devices will no longer be supported.
contents.html_ja: 製造者のコミュニケーションの不可欠な要素は、IoT デバイスのサイバーセキュリティに関する顧客の責任を明確に説明することです。たとえば消費者は主に、基本的な設置と構成のガイダンスを必要とするのに対し、組織の顧客は、デバイスの構成可能性、デバイスの大規模な展開、組織が法的義務を確実に満たせるようにする情報に対処する、より広範な文書を必要とします。すべての顧客は、利用できる製造者のコミュニケーションチャネル、ソフトウェア更新の頻度、そして特定の IoT デバイスがそれ以降サポートされなくなるサポート終了日について、明確さを必要とします。

contents.html: Takeaway 9: Security for IoT should be addressed using a risk management approach in concert with that used for traditional information technology, although different technical solutions may be needed for each.
contents.html_ja: 要点 9: IoT のセキュリティは、従来の情報技術に用いられるものと協調したリスクマネジメントのアプローチを用いて対処すべきです。ただし、それぞれに異なる技術的な解決策が必要となる場合があります。

contents.html: Workshop panelists agreed that IoT devices introduce varying amounts of risk into their environments. For example, IoT devices regulating physical access or supporting warning systems may represent much greater risk than so-called “smart” appliances; however, attacks using apparently low-risk devices (e.g., an aquarium thermometer, a network-connected traffic sign) as paths into owner information systems have had serious consequences. Detection and identification of the IoT devices present in an environment also presents a significant challenge. Information about individual devices can be difficult to obtain, although there are efforts to crowdsource such information to ease the challenge of device identification.
contents.html_ja: ワークショップのパネリストは、IoT デバイスが環境にもたらすリスクの大きさはさまざまであるという点で一致しました。たとえば、物理的なアクセスを制御するデバイスや警報システムを支えるデバイスは、いわゆる「スマート」家電よりはるかに大きなリスクを表す可能性があります。しかし、一見リスクの低いデバイス（たとえば水槽の温度計やネットワーク接続された交通標識）を所有者の情報システムへの経路として使った攻撃は、深刻な結果をもたらしています。環境内に存在する IoT デバイスの検知と識別も、大きな課題です。個々のデバイスに関する情報は入手が難しい場合がありますが、デバイス識別の課題を和らげるために、そうした情報をクラウドソーシングで集める取り組みもあります。

contents.html: The introduction of IoT devices may require a shift of mindset when applying the NIST Risk Management Framework (RMF). As stated by Grant Schneider: “Risk management: that's really what this boils down to.” System owners and assessors need to clearly understand guidance that federal information systems include IoT devices, which must be viewed as part of the enterprise information system and treated as components of the system(s) being assessed. Katherine Gronberg observed that a goal of federal programs “is ultimately to assess and then mitigate risk on the networks which include IoT and OT presence.” Agencies must ensure that IoT devices are included within the scope of their risk management approach, whether assessing enterprise IT, specific IT systems, or operational technology (OT) systems where IoT devices have been introduced. Security controls from the SP 800-53 catalog must be considered in the assessment of IoT devices within agency systems.
contents.html_ja: IoT デバイスの導入は、NIST リスクマネジメントフレームワーク（RMF）を適用する際に、考え方の転換を必要とする場合があります。Grant Schneider 氏が述べたように、「リスクマネジメント、結局のところ本当にそこに行き着きます。」システムの所有者と評価者は、連邦情報システムに IoT デバイスが含まれるというガイダンスを明確に理解する必要があります。IoT デバイスは、エンタープライズ情報システムの一部と見なされ、評価対象のシステムの構成要素として扱われなければなりません。Katherine Gronberg 氏は、連邦プログラムの目標は「最終的に、IoT と OT が存在するネットワークのリスクを評価し、軽減することです」と述べました。機関は、エンタープライズ IT、特定の IT システム、IoT デバイスが導入された運用技術（OT）システムのいずれを評価する場合でも、IoT デバイスがリスクマネジメントのアプローチの範囲に含まれることを確保しなければなりません。機関のシステム内の IoT デバイスの評価では、SP 800-53 カタログのセキュリティ管理策を考慮しなければなりません。

contents.html: No single security solution is appropriate for all devices across this spectrum. As IoT devices are integrated into federal information systems, potential issues arise regarding the ability to both understand and modify device configurations in order to bring them into alignment with security controls imposed by the RMF process (e.g., implementing a mandatory warning banner in the user interface of an IoT device).
contents.html_ja: この幅広い範囲のすべてのデバイスに適した単一のセキュリティ解決策はありません。IoT デバイスが連邦情報システムに統合されるにつれ、RMF のプロセスによって課されるセキュリティ管理策（たとえば IoT デバイスのユーザーインタフェースへの必須の警告バナーの実装）に合わせるために、デバイスの構成を理解し変更する能力に関する潜在的な問題が生じます。

contents.html: The introduction of IoT devices creates significant challenges for security assessment of federal information systems. Cybersecurity must be assessed both at the component level (i.e., individual IoT devices) and the system level (i.e., the integration of a set of IoT devices with traditional IT in a specific operating environment). An additional challenge is security testing of systems with IoT devices, especially when evaluating the impacts of updates to those devices. For example, if automatic security updates of IoT devices are enabled, when and by whom are tests of those updates to be performed?
contents.html_ja: IoT デバイスの導入は、連邦情報システムのセキュリティ評価に重大な課題をもたらします。サイバーセキュリティは、構成要素レベル（すなわち個々の IoT デバイス）と、システムレベル（すなわち特定の運用環境における一連の IoT デバイスと従来の IT との統合）の両方で評価されなければなりません。さらなる課題は、IoT デバイスを含むシステムのセキュリティテスト、特にそれらのデバイスの更新による影響の評価です。たとえば、IoT デバイスの自動セキュリティ更新が有効な場合、その更新のテストは、いつ、誰が実施するのでしょうか。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p16（scale 1.4、必要箇所は拡大）と照合。一致

contents.html: Software updates for IoT devices are a crucial aspect of cybersecurity. Automation of updating is generally one of the strongest mechanisms for minimizing device vulnerability and opportunities for attack, especially in the consumer space. Workshop participants favored automated update mechanisms that still offer device owners a measure of control over when updates are applied (poll #7). In the context of a federal information system, a complicating factor is the need to test updates prior to application due to their potential to affect a system’s security posture. In some cases, updates can significantly alter the capabilities of an IoT device (e.g., by activating hardware capabilities that have been latent), with correspondingly significant implications for the information system’s risk posture. Federal information system owners need to establish a process to assign responsibility for and establish an environment to enable testing of updates.
contents.html_ja: IoT デバイスのソフトウェア更新は、サイバーセキュリティの重要な側面です。更新の自動化は一般に、特に消費者分野で、デバイスの脆弱性と攻撃の機会を最小化する最も強力な仕組みの一つです。ワークショップの参加者は、更新がいつ適用されるかについてデバイスの所有者が一定の制御を保てる自動更新の仕組みを支持しました（アンケート #7）。連邦情報システムの文脈では、更新がシステムのセキュリティ態勢に影響しうるため、適用前に更新をテストする必要があることが複雑化の要因となります。場合によっては、更新が IoT デバイスの能力を大きく変えることがあり（たとえば、潜在していたハードウェア機能の有効化）、情報システムのリスク態勢にも、それに応じた重大な影響があります。連邦情報システムの所有者は、更新のテストに対する責任を割り当てるプロセスを確立し、そのテストを可能にする環境を整える必要があります。

contents.html: Takeaway 10: Securely integrating IoT devices into modern networks will require moving beyond legacy network security solutions.
contents.html_ja: 要点 10: IoT デバイスを現代的なネットワークに安全に統合するには、従来のネットワークセキュリティ解決策を超えていく必要があります。

contents.html: Network segmentation, traffic shaping with firewalls, and other legacy network security solutions are severely challenged by the introduction of IoT devices. IoT devices as elements of federal information systems may present very different security characteristics from traditional IT system elements, yet all must support the overall security goals and objectives for the complete information system. Bo Berlas observed “Traditionally we’ve been dependent on VLANS and firewalls and things of that nature, I think we need to go through and advance that understanding to start to look at for example with network access control tools, … looking at device profiling, … looking at newer concepts like zero trust.”
contents.html_ja: ネットワークのセグメンテーション、ファイアウォールによるトラフィックシェーピングなどの従来のネットワークセキュリティ解決策は、IoT デバイスの導入によって大きな課題に直面しています。連邦情報システムの要素としての IoT デバイスは、従来の IT システムの要素とは大きく異なるセキュリティ特性を持つ場合がありますが、すべてが情報システム全体のセキュリティの目的と目標を支えなければなりません。Bo Berlas 氏は次のように述べました。「従来、私たちは VLAN やファイアウォールなどに依存してきましたが、その理解を進めて、たとえばネットワークアクセス制御ツール、…デバイスのプロファイリング、…ゼロトラストのような新しい概念に目を向け始める必要があると思います。」

contents.html: The threat environment associated with IoT devices can be more dynamic than that associated with other products, including traditional IT products. For example, not all IoT devices support software updates to remove vulnerabilities. When software updates are possible, updates to deployed IoT devices can change their operational and cybersecurity characteristics. Such changes can, in turn, change the risk characteristics of the systems in which the devices are deployed. In parallel, attackers seek new avenues for exploitation of IoT devices as their characteristics evolve. The dynamic nature of IoT devices mitigates against the use of traditional product assessment and certification models for IoT devices; a one-time certification becomes meaningless as the device changes over time.
contents.html_ja: IoT デバイスに関連する脅威環境は、従来の IT 製品を含む他の製品に関連するものよりも動的である場合があります。たとえば、脆弱性を取り除くソフトウェア更新にすべての IoT デバイスが対応しているわけではありません。ソフトウェア更新が可能な場合でも、展開済みの IoT デバイスへの更新は、その運用上およびサイバーセキュリティ上の特性を変える可能性があります。そのような変化は、次に、デバイスが展開されているシステムのリスク特性を変える可能性があります。同時に、攻撃者は、IoT デバイスの特性が進化するにつれ、その悪用の新たな経路を探します。IoT デバイスの動的な性質は、従来の製品評価・認証モデルを IoT デバイスに用いることを妨げます。デバイスが時間とともに変化するため、一度きりの認証は意味をなさなくなります。

contents.html: Another challenge is dealing with security incidents involving devices performing critical functions. It may be unacceptable, for example, to completely quarantine a device that performs a mission critical function dependent on Internet connectivity. A related consideration is the loss of manufacturer support when Internet connectivity is withdrawn, both in terms of direct actions like software updates, and considerations of whether manufacturers honor product warranties.
contents.html_ja: もう一つの課題は、重要な機能を果たすデバイスが関わるセキュリティインシデントへの対処です。たとえば、インターネット接続に依存するミッションクリティカルな機能を果たすデバイスを完全に隔離することは、受け入れられない場合があります。関連する考慮事項として、インターネット接続が断たれたときの製造者の支援の喪失があります。これは、ソフトウェア更新のような直接的な措置と、製造者が製品保証を履行するかどうかという考慮事項の両方に関わります。

contents.html: When combined with edge computing concepts enabled by new technologies such as 5G, this creates difficulty in defining the boundaries of a federal information system by introducing system topologies that vary greatly from traditional models. This technology enables the expanded use of edge computing deployed outside the traditional boundaries that define federal information systems, as well as other “smart” solutions, both of which could create situations where 5G-enabled IoT devices may be capturing and processing federal data while being physically and/or logically outside the bounds of any particular federal information system.
contents.html_ja: 5G のような新技術によって可能になるエッジコンピューティングの概念と組み合わさると、従来のモデルとは大きく異なるシステムトポロジーが導入されるため、連邦情報システムの境界を定義することが困難になります。この技術は、連邦情報システムを定義する従来の境界の外に展開されるエッジコンピューティングや、その他の「スマート」ソリューションの利用拡大を可能にします。その両方が、5G に対応した IoT デバイスが、特定の連邦情報システムの境界の物理的、論理的、またはその両方の外側にありながら、連邦のデータを取得し処理している状況を生み出す可能性があります。

contents.html: Device discovery and on-boarding is a known major challenge with IoT devices. Katherine Gronberg stated that IoT devices are “actually very difficult to detect. It is actually hard, we find agencies don't know how much is actually on their networks.” Scott Rose observed “in order for IoT to succeed you cannot rely on individuals to set up and administer every individual IoT device. You will have to have this kind of autonomic network configuration.” Manufacturers and standards organizations have begun developing approaches to address some of these concerns:

contents.html: The supply chain represents both challenge and opportunity for IoT device cybersecurity. Grant Schneider stated that “supply chain risk management … [is of] significant interest both on the part of Congress and on the part of the executive branch.” The complexity and opacity of current IoT supply chains raises concerns about opportunities for bad actors to negatively impact device cybersecurity and a general inability for purchasers to have confidence in the characteristics of any particular product emerging from that supply chain. Apostolos Malatras noted that the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) has observed that, compared to other manufacturing sectors, “the relationship between suppliers and providers, between the peers in the supply chain are not mature at all. And they change very frequently.” However, there are also opportunities to share information gathered about the supply chain, and some organizations are focusing on the supply chain as a more effective place to focus cybersecurity efforts: rather than working to raise customer awareness they instead place pressure on manufacturers to configure their supply chains to produce more secure products. There is also potential for other mechanisms, such as third-party assessment and certifications and regulations requiring recall procedures, to have a positive impact on IoT device cybersecurity through the supply chain.
contents.html_ja: サプライチェーンは、IoT デバイスのサイバーセキュリティにとって課題でもあり機会でもあります。Grant Schneider 氏は、「サプライチェーンリスクマネジメントは、議会と行政府の双方にとって非常に関心の高い分野です」と述べました。現在の IoT サプライチェーンの複雑さと不透明さは、悪意ある者がデバイスのサイバーセキュリティに悪影響を及ぼす機会があることへの懸念と、そのサプライチェーンから生まれる個々の製品の特性について、購入者が一般に確信を持てないことへの懸念を高めています。Apostolos Malatras 氏は、欧州連合サイバーセキュリティ機関（ENISA）が、他の製造業の分野と比べ、「サプライヤーとプロバイダーの関係、サプライチェーン内の同業者どうしの関係は、まったく成熟していません。しかも、非常に頻繁に変わります」と観察していることを指摘しました。しかし、サプライチェーンについて収集された情報を共有する機会もあり、サイバーセキュリティの取り組みを集中させるより効果的な場所としてサプライチェーンに焦点を当てている組織もあります。それらの組織は、顧客の意識を高めるのではなく、製造者にサプライチェーンを構成してよりセキュアな製品を生み出すよう圧力をかけています。第三者による評価と認証や、リコール手順を義務づける規制など、ほかの仕組みにも、サプライチェーンを通じて IoT デバイスのサイバーセキュリティに好影響を与える可能性があります。

contents.html: A related idea is the concept of a labeling authority, a non-profit, non-governmental organization that would serve as a project manager for centralized certification and labeling efforts in the United States. The authority would accredit other organizations to take on specific IoT technology verticals, such as medical devices or connected automobiles. Mike Bergman noted that “The IoT ecosystem is enormous. It needs more than a single type of baseline and more than one type of confidence mechanism. In that broad landscape there is room for third-party assessment and supplier declaration of conformity for certification and labeling and so on.” Rob Morgus called participants’ attention to the U.S. Cyberspace Solarium Commission’s “recommendation for creation of a national cybersecurity certification and labeling authority. … It would be a nonprofit, nongovernmental organization to serve as a project manager for centralized certification and labeling efforts in the United States, empowered to accredit other organizations to sort of take on specific verticals of technology, like certain IoT verticals.”

The Information Technology Laboratory (ITL) at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) promotes the U.S. economy and public welfare by providing technical leadership for the Nation’s measurement and standards infrastructure. ITL develops tests, test methods, reference data, proof of concept implementations, and technical analyses to advance the development and productive use of information technology. ITL’s responsibilities include the development of management, administrative, technical, and physical standards and guidelines for the cost-effective security and privacy of other than national security-related information in federal information systems.

This report summarizes the feedback received on the work of the NIST Cybersecurity for IoT program on device cybersecurity at a virtual workshop in July 2020. NISTIR 8259, Foundational Cybersecurity Activities for IoT Device Manufacturers and NISTIR 8259A, IoT Device Cybersecurity Capability Core Baseline provide general guidance on how manufacturers can understand and approach their role in supporting customers’ cybersecurity needs and goals. As discussed in those documents, specific sectors and use cases may require more specific guidance than what is included in NISTIR 8259A’s core baseline for IoT devices. NIST conducted the virtual workshop “Building the Federal Profile for IoT Device Cybersecurity” to discuss and gather community input on the creation of a federal profile of the core baseline for use by federal agencies. This publication provides a summary of the workshop. The baseline will be published in NISTIR 8259D, Profile of the IoT Core Baseline for the Federal Government.

A.5 Most Promising Technical Approaches for Managing IoT Cybersecurity Risks
1 Introduction

On July 22-23, 2020, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) conducted a virtual workshop entitled Building the Federal Profile For IoT Device Cybersecurity: Next Steps for Securing Federal Systems. The event included stakeholders from across government, industry, international bodies, and academia. The goal was to identify gaps in the Internet of Things (IoT) cybersecurity ecosystem that need to be addressed in a federal profile for IoT device cybersecurity. Over 500 people participated from the U.S. and 25 other countries, representing a broad mix of government, industry, and academia.
1.1 About the NIST Cybersecurity for the Internet of Things Program

The mission of the NIST Cybersecurity for the Internet of Things (IoT) program [PRGM] is to cultivate trust in the IoT and foster an environment that enables innovation on a global scale through standards, guidance, and related tools. The Cybersecurity for IoT program supports the development and application of standards, guidelines, and related tools to improve the cybersecurity of connected devices and the environments in which they are deployed. By collaborating with stakeholders across government, industry, international bodies, and academia, the program aims to cultivate trust and foster an environment that enables innovation on a global scale.
1.2 Background For The Federal Profile

NIST leveraged the Core Baseline established in NIST Internal Report (NISTIR) 8259A, IoT Device Cybersecurity Capability Core Baseline [NISTIR8259A], and analyzed the security controls found in NIST Special Publication (SP) 800-53, Security and Privacy Controls for Federal Information Systems and Organizations [SP800-53], to develop a catalog of key IoT device cybersecurity capabilities and non-technical supporting capabilities and associated IoT device customer controls. As was discussed in NISTIR 8228, Considerations for Managing Internet of Things (IoT) Cybersecurity and Privacy Risks [NISTIR8228], IoT devices routinely lack critical cybersecurity capabilities that are commonly found in IT devices. Additionally, IoT manufacturers often do not provide sufficient information for IoT device customers to integrate their devices in secure ways in order to mitigate the risks created within the associated systems and to comply with compliance requirements. The catalog under development is a critical building block for establishing a federal profile of the Core Baseline (“federal profile”) to help federal agencies and manufacturers bridge these gaps. Identifying critically needed capabilities will help federal agencies acquire IoT devices that they can securely incorporate into their systems and meet security requirements for federal information and systems. The future federal profile also aims to help manufacturers looking at federal customers and use cases to go beyond identifying the types of cybersecurity device capabilities listed in NISTIR 8259A to considering specific capabilities requirements of federal agencies. Manufacturers can engineer the technical capabilities and provide non-technical supporting capabilities to IoT device customers to help ensure that customers’ systems meet an established level of management, operational, and technical security control requirements.
1.3 About the IoT Federal Profile Virtual Workshop

The free, publicly available virtual workshop consisted of a pair of two-hour long sessions, one per day1. The agenda is provided in Table 1. It included panel discussions on key topics related to cybersecurity challenges for federal IoT devices. These topics include the need for support for IoT device cybersecurity capabilities and additional supporting capabilities from the manufacturers and mechanisms giving federal agencies, as well as non-federal users of IoT devices, confidence that such devices will satisfy defined cybersecurity requirements.

NIST sought attendance from those involved in federal IoT cybersecurity, the manufacturers of IoT devices, researchers in related fields and other stakeholders. NIST encouraged participants to become familiar with the key IoT device cybersecurity capabilities and supporting non-technical manufacturer capabilities and associated IoT device customer controls previously developed by NIST and available for review and feedback via GitHub2.
The workshop drew approximately 500 participants, panelists, speakers, and moderators. This included representatives from:
A mixture of government, industry, and academia, as well as researchers and the press
A broad range of federal government organizations including civil government, defense, and intelligence
26 countries, including 5 foreign governments
At least 39 U.S. states, including 8 state governments

In addition to the ability for participants to submit individual questions (which could be “up-voted” by other participants), the workshop included a series of 12 polls as a mechanism to gather participant feedback and influence the focus of panel discussions. The poll questions and poll results are presented in Appendix A. Since workshop attendees created a by-definition self-selected survey group and poll responses were entirely voluntary, poll results should not be viewed as providing statistically-valid sample size results for their questions.

Videos of each workshop segment are available on the event web page. Based on the participant presentations and feedback collected from stakeholders, this report provides a summary of key points and a general discussion of possible follow-on activities for the program.

2 Event Summary and Key Takeaways
The summary below highlights significant points from the keynote presentation, and identifies discussion topics, and NIST’s takeaways and observations from the three panel sessions.
2.1 Keynote: Federal Chief Information Security Officer

The keynote presentation was made by Grant Schneider, the Federal Chief Information Security Officer (CISO), setting the stage for the panel discussions that followed. Mr. Schneider also participated in a question and answer session at the conclusion of his keynote. Mr. Schneider’s presentation and responses to questions highlighted a number of important considerations for the use of IoT technology in federal information systems:

In his opinion, IoT security has not received enough attention, in both consumer and organizational contexts. He noted that the increasing interconnection of systems of all types increases attack surfaces and expands the threat profile.

He identified three core activities that the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) performs that are particularly relevant to federal information system security: Overseeing the implementation of Federal Information Security Management Act o (FISMA) for non-National Security Systems; he noted that in doing this OMB works closely with the Department of Defense (DoD) and the Director of National Intelligence (DNI) to present consistent guidance across the federal space including the DoD and the intelligence community (IC). Overseeing the implementation of cybersecurity policies and standards. He noted o that OMB has been taking a more active oversight role and seeking to assist federal organizations in meeting their FISMA responsibilities. Ensuring agencies comply with government-wide cybersecurity guidance and o legislation, including Binding Operational Directives and Emergency Directives from the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

He stated that the scope of “Federal Information systems includes IoT devices”, adding “I don't think we've had enough conversation on that.” He expressed concern that IoT devices are seen as less impactful or less risky, and cited an example of a networked traffic sign being used as an entry point for a cyber-attack as a “wake-up call” to the range of concerns that IoT raises.

He emphasized that OMB’s work in cybersecurity is guided by a risk management philosophy. He described a “high-value asset” program intended to assist agencies in identifying and protecting their high-value information system and data, and share solutions across agencies.

He said the Federal government is seeking to lead by example, as captured in the National Cyber Strategy published in September 2018 [CYBSTRAT]. Concerns he identified included the difficulty of determining the security provided by IoT products, and the limitations of government buying power to “move the economy”, meaning that other incentives such as government mandates or regulation might need to be considered.

He indicated that IoT devices were a component of broader concerns about supply chain security and risk management, which is a major focus of both the executive and legislative branches of government. Poorly designed and configured devices are a notable part of that supply chain concern.

He described the creation of the Federal Acquisition Security Council (FASC) by the Secure Technologies Act of 2018 [SECTECH], and identified several FASC focus areas: The creation of an information sharing environment for supply chain risk o management information. The potential establishment of shared services for supply chain risk management, o to allow federal organizations of all sizes to perform due diligence regarding supply chain risk. Recommending removal orders or exclusion orders to DHS, DoD, and the IC to o ban covered items, and encouraging individual agencies to develop their own such orders where appropriate.

He clarified that IoT devices that connect via cloud or mobile (e.g., 5G) technologies are part of federal information systems even if they don’t directly touch a federal network, saying that current policies cover IoT and similar devices in the definition of a federal information system, although he recognized there may be need for amplifying guidance.

He stated that he saw value in third-party certifications for IoT cybersecurity, although he noted that it could be unclear what is actually being certified, and suggested that it may be more meaningful to certify the manufacturer’s development methodology rather than specific IoT products.
He discussed the value of an international trusted marketplace for IoT, and the importance of international standards and working with international partners to achieve that.
2.2 Summary and Takeaways from Panel Sessions

These takeaways are ideas that NIST heard from participants and that received significant support from attendees and/or panelists. This workshop was not a forum for developing consensus, so these takeaways represent themes repeatedly heard not a formal position of attendees or participants. While this document seeks to be thorough in reflecting the workshop discussions, a summary document cannot capture all the thoughts, opinions, and suggestions provided during the sessions. The topics, takeaways, and observations in this report do not represent specific NIST recommendations or guidance, but are intended to capture and summarize discussions from the workshop and viewpoints expressed by panelists and participants. These takeaways provide important feedback to the program and a basis for future conversations with the community.
